body.objective: Students will be able to present my product and process.
body.iCan: I can present my product and process.
successCriteria: I can explain my product and how it meets the criteria
I can describe my design process
I can present clearly to an audience
body.hook: On TV shows like Dragons' Den, inventors get about three minutes to explain what they made, why it matters and how they made it. The best products can still fail if nobody understands them. Communicating is part of designing.

study.title: Three-Minute Showcase
study.question: How do I share my product and process clearly?
study.passage:
Presentation structure (written for this lesson):
1. Hook (15 seconds): a question or fact that grabs attention. "Have you ever lost your page because your bookmark tore?"
2. The brief (20 seconds): who the client was and what they needed.
3. The product (45 seconds): show it and explain how it meets each criterion, with evidence from testing.
4. The process (60 seconds): planning, a problem you hit, feedback you used, and version 2.
5. Wrap-up (20 seconds): what you learned and one question for the audience.
Delivery tips: stand where everyone can see the product; speak slowly and loudly enough for the back row; look at different people; use notes as reminders, not a script.
Audience task: For each presentation, note one strength and one question.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

Rehearse with a partner and get one tip

study.product: Deliver your three-minute showcase, then write two sentences about one thing that went well and one thing you would change.

body.objective: Students will be able to connect skills to careers.
body.iCan: I can connect skills to careers.
successCriteria: I can name the skills I used in CTF challenges
I can explain what a transferable skill is
I can connect my skills to occupations in different career clusters
body.hook: You just measured, planned, cooked, tested and presented. Those same skills are used every day by nurses, chefs, carpenters, accountants and game designers. The question isn't whether you have career skills; it's which careers you have them for.

vocabulary.definition: Something you can do well because you have learned and practised it.
A skill useful in many jobs, such as communication or problem solving.
A skill for a specific task or tool, such as using a sewing machine.
The path of jobs and learning a person follows through life.
A group of related careers that share skills and knowledge.

study.title: Skills to Careers Map
study.question: How do the skills I use in CTF connect to real careers?
study.passage:
Case studies (written for this lesson):
Amira, pastry chef: measures accurately, follows food-safety rules, plans orders for a busy morning, adjusts recipes when customers give feedback.
Daniel, electrician (apprentice): reads plans, measures carefully, follows safety rules, troubleshoots problems, explains work to clients.
Sara, game designer: plans a project, sketches ideas, tests games with players, fixes bugs, presents to a team.
Omar, nurse: follows hygiene rules, measures doses precisely, communicates with patients and families, works in a team, keeps careful records.
Task: Highlight the skills each person uses. Circle any skill used by all four. Then list three skills you used in CTF challenges this year and match each to at least two occupations.

body.objective: Students will be able to reflect on my interests.
body.iCan: I can reflect on my interests.
successCriteria: I can reflect on what I learned in CTF challenges
I can describe how my interests and strengths have changed
I can set a goal for my next challenge
body.hook: Athletes watch video of their games. Musicians record practice. People who improve fastest are the ones who look back and ask: what worked, what didn't, and what next? Today you look back on your CTF year so far.

vocabulary.definition: Thinking carefully about your experiences to learn from them.
A collection of your work and reflections that shows your learning.
A goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
Improvement in skills or understanding over time.
A piece of work or evidence saved in a portfolio.

study.title: My CTF Portfolio
study.question: How have my interests and skills grown, and what do I want to try next?
study.passage:
Portfolio checklist (written for this lesson):
1. Artifacts: Choose three pieces of evidence, for example your criteria checklist, a photo of your snack, your test results table or your presentation cue cards.
2. Reflection for each artifact: What is it? What did I learn making it? What would I do differently?
3. Interest check: Re-take the interest inventory from the first lesson. Compare your scores. Which went up? Which went down? Why?
4. Strength check: Name two skills that are now strengths and one skill you want to grow.
5. Goal: Write one SMART goal for your next CTF challenge. Example: "In the next challenge, I will finish a first prototype by the end of lesson 2 so I have time to test and improve it."
6. Share: Show one artifact to a partner and explain your growth.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Name your strengths and a skill to grow
Write a SMART goal and share with a partner
discussion: Which artifact shows your biggest growth?
How have your interests changed since the start?
